answer.answer:
Yes — a married Singapore citizen with a Singapore PR spouse can buy a new HDB flat as an SC/SPR household, provided they meet HDB’s eligibility conditions. The HDB rules for couples and families cover households buying as a Singapore Citizen or Singapore Permanent Resident household [1]. For resale flats, any buyer and any member of the core family nucleus who are SPRs must have held SPR status for at least 3 years at the time of the HFE letter application [2].

For buying a flat from HDB, all applicants and occupiers listed in the HFE letter application must not own or have an interest in any local or overseas private residential property, and must not have disposed of any such property within 30 months before the HFE letter application [1]. They can own or have an interest in up to 1 non-residential property at the time of the HFE letter application; if they own more than 1, they must dispose of the others at least 30 months before the HFE letter application [1].

answer.answer:
Yes — a married Singapore citizen and Singapore PR spouse can fall under HDB’s “Couples and Families” category as an SC or SPR household, which is the framework used for buying a flat from HDB.[1]

For a new flat, they must still meet HDB’s eligibility conditions. In particular, all applicants and occupiers listed in the HFE letter application must not own or have an interest in any local or overseas private residential property, and must not have disposed of any private residential property within 30 months before the HFE letter application, counted from the legal completion date.[1]

The separate “non-resident spouse” category is for an SC buying with a spouse who is not an SC or SPR, so that is not the rule for an SPR spouse.[1]

At age 60, you may have a few possible HDB options, depending on whether you are buying alone or with someone else.

If you are buying on your own as a single Singapore citizen, HDB says singles aged 35 and above can buy a flat alone, and should apply for an HDB Flat Eligibility (HFE) letter to find out their eligibility to buy a new or resale flat, as well as any CPF housing grants and HDB housing loan they may qualify for. [2][3]

For people aged 55 and above, CPF’s guide says you can buy a short-lease 2-room Flexi flat from HDB, or buy any flat in the resale market. Community Care Apartments are only for those aged 65 and above. [4]

Since you specifically want a 3-room flat, the passages I have do not confirm a new 3-room flat option for a single buyer aged 60. I could only confirm that a 3-room flat may be possible in the resale market. [2][4]

If you want me to narrow this down, I need to know:
- are you buying alone, or with a spouse/parent/child? [2][5]
- if with a spouse, is your spouse a Singapore citizen, PR, or non-resident? [5]
- are you looking at a new flat or a resale flat? [2][4]
- do you want to use an HDB loan or bank loan? HDB says the HFE letter will assess this. [1][6]

At age 60, you may be able to buy a 3-room HDB flat in the resale market. Other possible options for someone aged 55 and above are a short-lease 2-room Flexi flat, and the seniors page is the relevant route if you are considering that.[2][3] A short-lease 2-room Flexi flat can have a lease between 15 and 45 years in 5-year steps, subject to the rule that it must cover the youngest owner using OA savings up to at least age 95.[3]

For financing, if you want an HDB housing loan, you must first apply for an HFE letter.[1] HDB says singles aged 35 and above may get an HDB housing loan when buying a 5-room or smaller resale flat, but HDB housing loans are not available for short-lease 2-room Flexi flats or Community Care Apartments.[1]

Also, are you looking at a resale 3-room flat or a short-lease senior flat, and do you want to use an HDB housing loan?[2][1] Please check the linked official pages for the latest position.

answer.answer:
A first-time married couple buying an HDB resale flat may qualify for these grants, if they meet the eligibility conditions:

1. **Family Grant** under the CPF Housing Grant Scheme for families buying a resale flat. HDB says families buying a resale flat may qualify for a housing subsidy of **up to $80,000**. For the Family Grant, at least 1 core member must be a first-timer, and first-timer core applicants/ occupiers must not have taken any housing subsidy before. This grant is for couples, families, or orphaned siblings who are first-timer applicants buying an HDB resale flat. [2]

2. **Enhanced CPF Housing Grant (EHG) for Families**. If you are a first-timer applicant, you may be eligible for the EHG for a new or resale flat. **From 20 August 2024**, first-timer families may qualify for an EHG of **up to $120,000**. If buying a resale flat, you must first qualify for the CPF Housing Grants for resale flats (Families) before you may be eligible for the EHG. [1]

3. **Proximity Housing Grant (PHG) for Families** if you meet its eligibility conditions. HDB states families buying a resale flat may also apply for PHG if eligible. [1][2]

Also, if one spouse had earlier taken a Singles Grant or bought a 2-room/ 2-room Flexi flat from HDB as a single and is now married, the couple may apply for a **Top-Up Grant** instead, subject to the stated conditions. Check the linked HDB pages for the latest rules. [2]

answer.answer:
Plan for both cash and CPF at different stages of the resale purchase; HDB says you should ensure you have sufficient funds for all required payments.[2]

If you are taking a housing loan from a financial institution (bank/FI), at least 5% of the initial payment must be paid in cash.[2] CPF says this as a 5% cash downpayment for a bank loan, with the remaining 20% of the downpayment payable using CPF savings.[1]

You may use CPF savings for the initial payment.[2] If you are taking an HDB housing loan, you and each co-applicant may retain up to $20,000 in your CPF Ordinary Account, and the rest of the available OA balances must be used for the flat purchase.[2]

There is also a cash payment of $120 for the Request for Value if you intend to use CPF savings and/or a housing loan to buy the resale flat, unless otherwise advised by the FI.[2]

answer.answer:
Plan for both cash and CPF at different stages.

Upfront cash: you must pay the seller a deposit during the Option to Purchase (OTP) stage. This deposit is the Option Fee plus Option Exercise Fee, and the total must be between $2 and $5,000. More specifically, the Option Fee is between $1 and $1,000, and the total deposit cannot exceed $5,000. This forms part of the resale price. HDB says cash is required at the OTP stage. [2][3]

You also need cash for the resale application fee: $80, or $40 for 1- and 2-room flats. If you are using CPF savings and/or a housing loan, a Request for Value costs $120, unless otherwise advised by the financial institution. Legal fees are also payable, with the amount depending on the solicitor you appoint. [2]

For the initial payment, you may use CPF savings. If you take a bank/financial institution loan, at least 5% of the initial payment must be paid in cash; the remaining 20% can be paid using CPF savings. If your CPF savings are insufficient, part of the initial payment must also be in cash. [1][2]

CPF housing grants, if you are eligible, can be used for the initial payment and to reduce the loan amount. You must also pay any balance not covered by CPF savings, grants and the eligible loan amount before or during completion. Stamp duties are payable, and if HDB requires part of them in cash, you must pay that in cash. Check the latest official pages before you commit. [2][4]

Document: Help - Resale Procedures
Section: Help - Resale Procedures

6.1 If there is a recess area space fronting the flat available for sale, the buyers may request HDB to process the application to buy the recess area together with the resale application. The buyers must [write to us](https://www.hdb.gov.sg/write-to-us) to request information on the availability of the recess area for purchase at least 2 weeks before submitting the resale application. As the resale completion date may be affected/delayed, the seller’s consent will need to be obtained before HDB can process the 2 applications concurrently. In the absence of the seller’s consent, HDB will process the resale application without the purchase of the recess area.

**7 RESALE APPLICATION**

How much CPF savings you can use for your home purchase

Learn more about the amount of CPF OA savings you can use to purchase a home.

*4 Aug 2025*

*SOURCE: CPF Board*

There is a limit on how much of your CPF Ordinary Account (OA) savings can be used for a home purchase. This is so that you would have enough for your retirement.

This limit differs based on the valuation of the flat at time of purchase, purchase price, type of property, loan type, and age of property.

If the remaining lease of the flat can last the youngest owner until age 95, the amount of CPF savings you can use is capped at the lower of the purchase price and the valuation price at the time of purchase.

Your CPF savings can be used for purchasing a home, but did you know that there are limits in place?

Read on to learn more about using your CPF savings for a home purchase.

Section: Terms and conditions for use of CPF under the CPF Housing Scheme > 1. Application of terms and conditions > Part B - Terms and conditions for use of CPF for private residential properties under the CPF Housing Scheme > 1. Use of CPF savings
Part/Chapter: Part B

1. Use of CPF savings

a. You may use your CPF Ordinary Account (“**OA**”) savings for the following:

i. Direct payment of the purchase price of your private residential property to the property developer or sellers;

ii. Repayment of the housing loan in part or whole and/or to pay the monthly instalment of the housing loan taken for the purchase of your property, land and/or for construction of a house on that land; and/or

iii. Payment of the stamp duty, legal fees and other related costs incurred by you in connection with the purchase or mortgage of the property and/or construction of the house.

b. CPF savings cannot be used for the following:

i. Payment of option fees to property developers or sellers;

ii. Payment of construction works, improvements, repairs and/or renovation of your private residential property;

iii. Payment of monthly service and conservancy charges including all rates, taxes and other charges imposed on your private residential property;

iv. Repayment of non-housing loans (i.e. loans not taken for the purchase of your private residential property) and miscellaneous cost (i.e. penalties, insurance charges); or

v. Payment of purchase price that is above the lower of the purchase price or the valuation price of the property at the time of purchase for resale private residential property; and/or

vi. Reimbursement of any payments made to the property developers or sellers out of your personal funds in respect of the purchase of your private residential property.

The HPS is a mortgage-reducing insurance scheme offered by the CPF Board.

The [Home Protection Scheme (HPS)](https://www.cpf.gov.sg/member/home-ownership/protecting-against-losing-your-home) is a mortgage-reducing insurance scheme administered by the CPF Board and will take effect after your housing loan is disbursed. It insures CPF members and their families against losing their home, should the policy holder become permanently incapacitated or pass away before the housing loan is paid up. The HPS will settle the outstanding housing loan up to the insured sum, based on the share of cover applied.

HPS is compulsory if you use CPF savings to pay for your housing loan instalments.

The premium is paid annually using your CPF OA savings and/ or cash. You may estimate the premium of your HPS cover using the CPF Board's [HPS premium calculator](https://www.cpf.gov.sg/member/tools-and-services/calculators/home-protection-scheme-premium-calculator).

answer.answer:
Home Protection Scheme (HPS) is for CPF members who own an HDB flat and are paying monthly housing instalments using CPF savings or cash. It covers them until age 65 or until the housing loan is fully paid, whichever is earlier [1].

If you use CPF savings to pay your housing loan instalments, HPS is compulsory [2]. HPS takes effect after the housing loan is disbursed [2].

The key exception is that you may apply to be exempted from HPS if you already have equivalent private life insurance coverage [1]. The accepted policy types include Whole Life, Term Life, Endowment, Life Riders attached to a basic policy, and Mortgage Reducing Term Assurance / Decreasing Term Rider [1]. That private insurance must cover the outstanding housing loan for the full loan term or until age 65, whichever is earlier [1].

For the exemption process, you should first apply for HPS to avoid delays in using CPF savings for monthly instalments, and the exemption application can be made only after you have legal ownership of the flat and the housing loan has been disbursed [1]. The application must be submitted through your insurer, not directly by you [1].

Please check the linked CPF/HDB pages for the latest position.

Document: CPFB | T&C for use of CPF under CPF Housing Scheme
Section: Terms and conditions for use of CPF under the CPF Housing Scheme > 1. Application of terms and conditions > Part C - Standard terms and conditions > 2. Use of CPF saving for Multiple Property purchase
Part/Chapter: Part C

2. Use of CPF saving for Multiple Property purchase

a. There are additional restrictions if you have used your CPF savings for a property and are applying to use your CPF savings for a second or subsequent property (“**Multiple Property**”).

b. For Multiple Property bought from 1 July 2006 but before 10 May 2019:

i. You are required to set aside the latest BRS before you can use the excess savings in your OA for the Multiple Property;

ii. The maximum amount of CPF that can be used for your Multiple Property is capped at:

• Lower of the purchase price or the valuation price of the property at the time of purchase for property with a remaining lease of at least 60 years at the time of purchase; or

• A percentage of the lower of the purchase price or the valuation price of the property at the time of purchase for property with a remaining lease of less than 60 years but at least 30 years at the time of purchase.

c. For Multiple Property bought from 10 May 2019:

i. You are required to set aside the following before you can use the excess savings in your OA for the Multiple Property

• The latest BRS if you have at least one property bought using CPF or the property that you are buying can cover you till age 95*

• The latest Full Retirement Sum (“FRS”) if you do not have any property that can cover you till age 95

* If you subsequently sell the property that can cover you till age 95, you will need to set aside the FRS instead.

Section: FAQs

The amount of CPF Ordinary Account (OA) savings you can use depends on:

Remaining lease of the property

Type of property

Loan type

Whether it’s your first or subsequent property

Note: For members age 55 and above, your Basic Retirement Sum (BRS) is [half of your Full Retirement Sum](https://www.cpf.gov.sg/service/article/how-much-is-my-basic-retirement-sum) (FRS) which depends on the year you turn 55 and will remain the same for life. For members below 55, your BRS is half of the prevailing FRS in the year.

You can use our [CPF Housing Usage Calculator](https://www.cpf.gov.sg/member/tools-and-services/calculators/cpf-housing-usage) to determine the total amount of CPF savings that you and your co-owner (if any) may use to buy your property.

CPF savings used to pay for stamp duty, legal fees and upgrading costs are not included in the CPF housing limit.

Purchasing your second or subsequent property

You can only use your OA savings after setting aside the BRS or FRS (refer to Table B), up to the CPF housing limit of your property.

Table B: Amount to set aside

answer.answer:
The key CPF restriction is this: for a second or subsequent property, you can use CPF OA only after setting aside the required retirement sum, and the amount depends on whether you have a property that can cover you till age 95. If you have at least one property bought using CPF, or the property you are buying can cover you till age 95, you must set aside the latest BRS first; if you do not have any property that can cover you till age 95, you must set aside the latest FRS first.[2][3]

Because you are 58, your BRS is half of your FRS, based on the year you turned 55, and it stays the same for life.[3]

CPF use also depends on the property’s remaining lease, property type, loan type, and whether this is your first or subsequent property.[3] For members 55 and above buying a 3-room or smaller HDB flat, you may also use excess RA savings if you have already set aside your prevailing BRS.[5]

Cash still matters: some costs are not payable with CPF, including resale levy if this is your second subsidised flat, agent’s commission, and renovation costs.[1]

What’s missing to tell which restriction applies to you: whether this is your second or subsequent property bought using CPF, whether you still own any property, whether any such property can cover you till age 95, the new home’s lease, type and loan type, and whether it is a 3-room-or-smaller HDB flat.[2][3][5]

You can use the CPF Housing Usage Calculator and Home Purchase Planner to check the CPF limits and retirement impact. Please check the latest official page before acting.[1][3]

evidence.title: CPFB | How much do I need to refund to my CPF account when selling/transferring my property?
evidence.text:
Document: CPFB | How much do I need to refund to my CPF account when selling/transferring my property?
Section: FAQs

To check the exact amount that you need to refund your CPF accounts if you sell/transfer your property, simply log in to your [Home ownership dashboard](https://www.cpf.gov.sg/homeownershipdashboard) and look under the “What Happens If” section.

In general, the amount you must refund is the principal you have withdrawn for your property (P) and the accrued interest (I), i.e. “P+I”. If you are age 55 or above and have pledged your property to set aside your retirement sum, you must also refund the pledged amount.

**IMPORTANT NOTE:**

However, please note that your required CPF refund is less than your P+I if you:

were age 55 or older before 1 January 2013; and

have set aside your Full Retirement Sum (FRS) before 1 January 2013.

This is because having set aside your FRS before 1 January 2013, you are not required by law to refund the CPF you have used to pay for your property prior to 2013. If you have continued to use your CPF from 1 January 2013, only the principal amount used from 1 January 2013 and the accrued interest need to be refunded when you sell your property.

answer.answer:
The key CPF restriction is this: for a second or subsequent property, you can use CPF OA only after setting aside the required retirement sum, and then only up to the CPF housing limit for that property [1].

Because you are 58, the amount to set aside is tied to your retirement sum position at age 55 and above. CPF says your BRS is half of your FRS, based on the year you turned 55, and it stays the same for life [1]. CPF also says members aged 55 and above can check on the Retirement Dashboard whether they have set aside their FRS [2].

Other CPF limits also depend on facts not given here: the property's remaining lease, the type of property, the loan type, and whether this is your first or subsequent property [1]. I couldn't find the exact CPF amount you can use without those details [1].

Another fact that may matter is whether you own a Singapore property whose remaining lease lasts you to age 95 or older. If so, you may apply to withdraw RA savings down to your BRS [2].

If you will sell or transfer another property, CPF says the usual refund is the principal withdrawn plus accrued interest, and if you are 55 or above and pledged the property for your retirement sum, the pledged amount must also be refunded [3]. Please check the linked CPF pages for the latest position.
